problem: The scenario says an exchange 'co-spends withdrawals from many customers in one transaction'. Withdrawals are outputs: the inputs in such a batch are the exchange's own hot-wallet coins, so clustering them correctly gives one owner (the exchange) and does not falsely merge customers. The described false cluster only happens the other way round, when the exchange sweeps many customers' deposit addresses together as inputs.
fix: An exchange sweeps deposits from many customers' addresses into one transaction. How can this mislead clustering? Answer: the common-input heuristic may label all those customers as one owner, creating a false cluster; an analyst must treat the link as probabilistic.

problem: Calling CoinJoin simply 'trustless' hides a real point: most implementations use a coordinator. The coordinator cannot take the coins, but in unblinded designs it can learn which output belongs to which participant.
fix: CoinJoin is trustless in the sense that no operator holds the coins: several users build one transaction with many inputs and many equal-value outputs. Many implementations use a coordinator that cannot steal funds but may learn the input-output mapping unless the round is blinded.
